claim: Whale-watching comprises the largest component of marine mammal-based tourism, and the multi-billion-dollar industry is increasing globally.
source: Whale-watching comprises the largest component of marine mammal-based tourism, and the multi-billion-dollar industry is increasing globally (Hoyt, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hoyt, 2018

claim: Commercial whale-watching began in 1955.
source: Commercial whale-watching began in 1955 and has previously been viewed as a non-invasive activity that can generate a revenue for local economies as an alternative to whaling whilst allowing depleted whale stocks to recover.
evidence: Stated as historical fact in the manuscript

claim: Boat-based whale-watching can have short-term behavioural impacts on individuals.
source: It is, however, increasingly clear that boat-based whale-watching can have short-term behavioural impacts on individuals (New et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to New et al., 2015

claim: Short-term behavioural impacts of whale-watching include alterations of dive patterns, swim speeds, swim orientation, group cohesiveness, behavioural state and changes in acoustic behaviour.
source: Short-term behavioural impacts include alterations of dive patterns, swim speeds, swim orientation, group cohesiveness, behavioural state and changes in acoustic behaviour (for reviews see Senigaglia et al., 2016; Machernis et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to review papers by Senigaglia et al., 2016 and Machernis et al., 2018

claim: Repeated behavioural disruptions on individuals can lead to long-term negative effects on health, survival and reproduction.
source: Repeated behavioural disruptions on individuals can lead to long-term negative effects on health (i.e. body condition), survival and reproduction, which in turn, if a sufficient number of individuals are affected, can negatively influence population dynamics (Bejder et al., 2006; Lusseau et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bejder et al., 2006 and Lusseau et al., 2006

claim: Current whale-watching guidelines typically stipulate approach distance of ~100 m.
source: By stipulating approach distance (typically ~100 m), angle (typically from the rear and side), speed (typically below wake speed), current guidelines rest on the premise that physical proximity is the primary vehicle of disturbance (Higham et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Higham et al., 2014

claim: Current whale-watching guidelines rest on the premise that physical proximity is the primary vehicle of disturbance.
source: By stipulating approach distance (typically ~100 m), angle (typically from the rear and side), speed (typically below wake speed), current guidelines rest on the premise that physical proximity is the primary vehicle of disturbance (Higham et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Higham et al., 2014 and inference from guideline structure

claim: Whales in most waters of the world are offered no underwater visual cues at a range of 100 m.
source: Given that whales in most waters of the world are offered no underwater visual cues at a range of 100 m, it therefore seems plausible that hearing rather than vision is the sensory modality that serves to mediate behavioural responses to approaching whale-watch vessels.
evidence: Based on general knowledge about underwater visibility and whale vision

claim: Hearing rather than vision is the sensory modality that serves to mediate behavioural responses to approaching whale-watch vessels.
source: Given that whales in most waters of the world are offered no underwater visual cues at a range of 100 m, it therefore seems plausible that hearing rather than vision is the sensory modality that serves to mediate behavioural responses to approaching whale-watch vessels.
evidence: Inference based on limited underwater visibility and whale sensory capabilities

claim: 42 controlled exposure experiments were conducted on humpback whale mother-calf pairs.
source: To do this, we measured behavioural responses of 42 humpback whale (Megaptera novaeangliae) mother-calf pairs to different levels of vessel noise during controlled exposure experiments on a resting ground with murky waters excluding visual cues.
evidence: Stated as the sample size in the study

claim: The humpback whale is the most targeted species for whale-watching and swim-with-whale activities globally.
source: The humpback whale was used as a model species as it is the most targeted species for whale-watching and swim-with-whale activities globally, mainly due to its cosmopolitan distribution and highly acrobatic visual displays (Hendrix and Rose, 2014; Hoyt, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hendrix and Rose, 2014 and Hoyt, 2018

claim: Fieldwork was conducted in Exmouth Gulf, Western Australia, from August 1 to October 31 2018.
source: Fieldwork was conducted in Exmouth Gulf, Western Australia (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; between 21°45′–22°33′ S and 114°08′–114°40′ E), from August 1 to October 31 2018.
evidence: Stated as the study location and time period

claim: Humpback whales enter Exmouth Gulf during their southern migration, between late August and early November.
source: Humpback whales enter the Gulf during their southern migration, between late August and early November.
evidence: Stated as a fact about whale migration patterns in the study area

claim: Exmouth Gulf is an important resting ground for mother and calves.
source: The Gulf is an important resting ground for mother and calves, that may rest and nurse for a few weeks before continuing their southern migration to their high latitude feeding grounds (Jenner et al., 2001; Bestley et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jenner et al., 2001 and Bestley et al., 2019

claim: The Western Australian whale population is estimated to comprise 20–30,000 whales, increasing 9–12.7% yr−1.
source: The Western Australian whale population has increased substantially since the cessation of whaling and is estimated to comprise 20–30,000 whales, increasing 9–12.7% yr−1 (Bejder et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bejder et al., 2016

claim: Exmouth Gulf is shallow, with a mean water depth of 9 m and maximum of 20 m.
source: The Gulf is shallow, with a mean water depth of 9 m and maximum of 20 m.
evidence: Stated as a characteristic of the study site

claim: The soundscape in Exmouth Gulf is dominated by biological sounds, such as the continuous melody of male humpback whale song and omnipresent snapping shrimp, with minimal noise from anthropogenic activities.
source: The soundscape in the Gulf is dominated by biological sounds, such as the continuous melody of male humpback whale song and omnipresent snapping shrimp, with minimal noise from anthropogenic activities, such as vessels (Bejder et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bejder et al., 2019

claim: Vessel noise was played through a laptop, amplifier, bridging transformer box and emitted through an underwater acoustic transducer.
source: Vessel noise was played through a laptop (Acer Aspire ES 15), amplifier (Boss PM2500 monoblock), bridging transformer box (AC1424 HP) and emitted through an underwater acoustic transducer (Lubell LL1424, flat [±3 dB] frequency range 200 Hz-9 kHz).
evidence: Description of the experimental equipment used

claim: The transducer was suspended from the side of the vessel to 1.5 m below the surface to mimic typical depth of propellers/shaft/exhaust of whale-watching vessels.
source: The transducer was suspended from the side of the vessel to 1.5 m below the surface to mimic typical depth of propellers/shaft/exhaust of whale-watching vessels (Figure 1B).
evidence: Description of experimental setup with reference to Figure 1B

claim: Vessel noise was emitted with a 60 s ramp up/down to avoid an acoustic startle response from the whales.
source: Vessel noise was emitted with a 60 s ramp up/down to avoid an acoustic startle response from the whales.
evidence: Description of experimental protocol

claim: Vessel noise was set to different LF-weighted broadband source levels of control (124 dB re 1 μPa), low (148 dB re 1 μPa), medium (160 dB re 1 μPa) and high noise (172 dB re 1 μPa RMS).
source: Vessel noise was set to different LF-weighted broadband source levels (SLs) of control (124 dB re 1 μPa), low (148 dB re 1 μPa), medium (160 dB re 1 μPa) and high noise (172 dB re 1 μPa RMS).
evidence: Description of experimental treatments

claim: The research vessel noise SL was calculated at 140 ± 2 dB re 1 μPa low frequency (LF)-weighted.
source: The research vessel noise SL was calculated at 140 ± 2 dB re 1 μPa low frequency (LF)-weighted (Southall et al., 2019).
evidence: Measurement of the research vessel's source level

claim: Selected noise levels represent a range of slow moving (<10 knts) motorised whale-watch vessels that a whale would experience in the wild, having SLs ranging from 138 to 169 dB re 1 μPa @ 1 m.
source: These selected noise levels represent a range of slow moving (<10 knts) motorised whale-watch vessels that a whale would experience in the wild, having SLs ranging from 138 to 169 dB re 1 μPa @ 1 m (Jensen et al., 2009; Wladichuk et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jensen et al., 2009 and Wladichuk et al., 2019

claim: The control was set to 124 dB re 1 μPa to ensure it was ~16 dB quieter than the vessel noise at 800 rpm.
source: The control was set to 124 dB re 1 μPa to ensure it was ~16 dB quieter than the vessel noise at 800 rpm.
evidence: Description of experimental design rationale

claim: Controlled exposure experiments consisted of a before, during and after experimental design.
source: Controlled exposure experiments consisted of a before, during and after experimental design (before phase = absence of vessel, stationary >300–400 m from whales with engine in neutral; during phase = vessel approach (Figure 1); after phase = departure of vessel, stationary >300 m from whales with engine in neutral).
evidence: Description of experimental design

claim: UAVs were flown at 25–30 m altitude.
source: UAVs were flown at 25–30 m altitude and positioned above the mother, facing north and the camera vertically down (Nielsen et al., 2019).
evidence: Description of UAV flight protocol with citation to Nielsen et al., 2019

claim: At 25-30 m altitudes, the presence of the UAV has no negative noise effects due to the low RLs underwater.
source: At these altitudes, the presence of the UAV has no negative noise effects due to the low RLs underwater (Christiansen et al., 2016b), and cause no apparent behavioural changes on baleen whales (Christiansen et al., 2020), thus this technology is non-invasive and appropriate to record undisturbed (control) behavioural responses.
evidence: Supported by citations to Christiansen et al., 2016b and Christiansen et al., 2020

claim: UAVs cause no apparent behavioural changes on baleen whales.
source: At these altitudes, the presence of the UAV has no negative noise effects due to the low RLs underwater (Christiansen et al., 2016b), and cause no apparent behavioural changes on baleen whales (Christiansen et al., 2020), thus this technology is non-invasive and appropriate to record undisturbed (control) behavioural responses.
evidence: Supported by citation to Christiansen et al., 2020

claim: An increase in instantaneous behaviours is an indicator of disturbance to whale-watching activities.
source: An increase in instantaneous behaviours is an indicator of disturbance to whale-watching activities (Machernis et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Machernis et al., 2018

claim: During whale-watch interactions the respiration rate of minke whales increased, irrespective of swim speed, indicating an increase in metabolic rate.
source: Respiration rate relates to energy expenditure, for example, during whale-watch interactions the respiration rate of minke whales increased, irrespective of swim speed, indicating an increase in metabolic rate (Christiansen et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Christiansen et al., 2014

claim: Controlled exposure experiments were conducted across 53 days from 25 August to 28 October, 2018.
source: Controlled exposure experiments were conducted across 53 days (290 hr on the water) from 25 August to 28 October, 2018 (Figure 2).
evidence: Stated as the duration of field work with reference to Figure 2

claim: Vessel track lines searching for resting mother-calf pairs covered 2337 km.
source: Vessel track lines searching for resting mother-calf pairs covered 2337 km (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated as the total distance covered with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Over 60 CEEs were conducted, including 273 UAV flights (78 hr of flight time).
source: Over 60 CEEs were conducted, including 273 UAV flights (78 hr of flight time).
evidence: Stated as the total number of experiments and flights

claim: The length of mothers ranged from 9.7 m to 16.7 m (mean = 13.2 m; n = 105).
source: The length of mothers ranged from 9.7 m to 16.7 m (mean = 13.2 m; n = 105), and for calves from 4.5 m to 8.4 m (mean = 6.3 m; n = 104; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated as measured data with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: The length of calves ranged from 4.5 m to 8.4 m (mean = 6.3 m; n = 104).
source: The length of mothers ranged from 9.7 m to 16.7 m (mean = 13.2 m; n = 105), and for calves from 4.5 m to 8.4 m (mean = 6.3 m; n = 104; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated as measured data with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: After data filtering, 13 control/low, 14 medium and 15 high noise CEEs were used in analyses (42 mother-calf pairs).
source: After data filtering, 13 control/low (including 4 low), 14 medium and 15 high noise CEEs were used in analyses (42 mother-calf pairs; Figure 2; Video 1 for examples of reactions).
evidence: Stated as the final sample size after filtering with references to Figure 2 and Video 1

claim: Control and low noise treatments were pooled as the RLs of vessel noise were around ambient noise.
source: Control and low noise treatments were pooled as the RLs of vessel noise were around ambient noise (Figure 3).
evidence: Stated as the rationale for pooling treatments with reference to Figure 3

claim: The average closest point of approach was 135 m (56.0 SD).
source: The average closest point of approach was 135 m (56.0 SD).
evidence: Stated as measured data from the experiments

claim: All treatments had a peak level in the third octave band around 4 kHz.
source: From the transiting calibration, all treatments had a peak level in the third octave band around 4 kHz, with mean LF-weighted RLs @100 m of: control at 104 dB, low noise at 112 dB (±1) (average distance: 103 m, range: 102–103 m), medium noise at 122 ± 3 dB (average distance: 102 m, range: 94–108 m), and high noise at 133 ± 2 dB (average distance: 101 m, range: 85–113 m) re 1 μPa RMS (0.125 s) (Figure 3; Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for shallower depth).
evidence: Stated as measured data with reference to Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Mean LF-weighted RL at 100 m for control was 104 dB re 1 μPa RMS.
source: From the transiting calibration, all treatments had a peak level in the third octave band around 4 kHz, with mean LF-weighted RLs @100 m of: control at 104 dB, low noise at 112 dB (±1) (average distance: 103 m, range: 102–103 m), medium noise at 122 ± 3 dB (average distance: 102 m, range: 94–108 m), and high noise at 133 ± 2 dB (average distance: 101 m, range: 85–113 m) re 1 μPa RMS (0.125 s) (Figure 3; Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for shallower depth).
evidence: Stated as measured data with reference to Figure 3

claim: Mean LF-weighted RL at 100 m for low noise was 112 ± 1 dB re 1 μPa RMS.
source: From the transiting calibration, all treatments had a peak level in the third octave band around 4 kHz, with mean LF-weighted RLs @100 m of: control at 104 dB, low noise at 112 dB (±1) (average distance: 103 m, range: 102–103 m), medium noise at 122 ± 3 dB (average distance: 102 m, range: 94–108 m), and high noise at 133 ± 2 dB (average distance: 101 m, range: 85–113 m) re 1 μPa RMS (0.125 s) (Figure 3; Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for shallower depth).
evidence: Stated as measured data with reference to Figure 3

claim: Mean LF-weighted RL at 100 m for medium noise was 122 ± 3 dB re 1 μPa RMS.
source: From the transiting calibration, all treatments had a peak level in the third octave band around 4 kHz, with mean LF-weighted RLs @100 m of: control at 104 dB, low noise at 112 dB (±1) (average distance: 103 m, range: 102–103 m), medium noise at 122 ± 3 dB (average distance: 102 m, range: 94–108 m), and high noise at 133 ± 2 dB (average distance: 101 m, range: 85–113 m) re 1 μPa RMS (0.125 s) (Figure 3; Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for shallower depth).
evidence: Stated as measured data with reference to Figure 3

claim: Mean LF-weighted RL at 100 m for high noise was 133 ± 2 dB re 1 μPa RMS.
source: From the transiting calibration, all treatments had a peak level in the third octave band around 4 kHz, with mean LF-weighted RLs @100 m of: control at 104 dB, low noise at 112 dB (±1) (average distance: 103 m, range: 102–103 m), medium noise at 122 ± 3 dB (average distance: 102 m, range: 94–108 m), and high noise at 133 ± 2 dB (average distance: 101 m, range: 85–113 m) re 1 μPa RMS (0.125 s) (Figure 3; Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for shallower depth).
evidence: Stated as measured data with reference to Figure 3

claim: Ambient noise was mostly dominated by humpback whale song and snapping shrimp.
source: Ambient noise was mostly dominated by humpback whale song and snapping shrimp (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Stated as observation with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: Median LF-weighted levels increased by a moderate 5 dB from 103 to 108 dB re 1uPa RMS (0.125 s).
source: Median LF-weighted levels increased by a moderate 5 dB from 103 to 108 dB re 1uPa RMS (0.125 s).
evidence: Stated as measured data

claim: The TOLs between 400 Hz and 2500 Hz rose by 10–15 dB as singing humpback whale males arrived through the breeding season.
source: However, the TOLs between 400 Hz and 2500 Hz rose by 10–15 dB as singing humpback whale males arrived through the breeding season (Figure 3), whereas high frequency TOLs changed little due to the ever-present snapping shrimp noise.
evidence: Stated as measured data with reference to Figure 3

claim: There were no significant effects for the proportion of time resting for the mother across phases within control/low and medium treatments.
source: There were no significant effects for the proportion of time resting for the mother across phases within control/low and medium treatments (GLMM-PQL logit scale: R2(m) = 0.09, R2(c) = 0.22; 126 phases; Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated as statistical result with references to Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Within high noise treatments, the proportion of time resting from before to during vessel approaches decreased significantly (p=0.02), with a 27% decrease in resting.
source: Within high noise treatments, the proportion of time resting from before to during vessel approaches decreased significantly (p=0.02,), with a 27% decrease in resting (Figure 4A).

claim: Among treatments, the proportion of time resting for the mother decreased significantly from during control/low to during medium (p=0.03, 23% decrease) and during high (p=0.01, 30% decrease) treatments.
source: Among treatments, the proportion of time resting for the mother decreased significantly from during control/low to during medium (p=0.03, 23% decrease) and during high (p=0.01, 30% decrease) treatments.
evidence: Stated as statistical result

claim: There were no significant effects within treatments on the proportion of time resting for the calf.
source: There were no significant effects within treatments on the proportion of time resting for the calf, for example, between before to during and before to after phases (GLMM-PQL logit scale: R2(m) = 0.08, R2(c) = 0.25; 126 phases; Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated as statistical result with references to Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Among treatments, the proportion of time resting for the calf decreased significantly between during control/low to during medium (p=0.02, 36% decrease) and during high (p=0.005, 49% decrease) treatments.
source: Among treatments, the proportion of time resting for the calf decreased significantly between during control/low to during medium (p=0.02, 36% decrease) and during high (p=0.005, 49% decrease) treatments.

claim: The presence of instantaneous behavioural events did not differ significantly across phases within control/low, medium and high treatments for the mother.
source: The presence of events did not differ significantly across phases within control/low, medium and high treatments (GLMM-PQL logit scale: R2(m) = 0.11, R2(c) = 0.39; 126 phases; Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated as statistical result with references to Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Among treatments, the presence of events differed significantly from during control/low to during medium treatments (p=0.02) for the mother.
source: Among treatments, the presence of events differed significantly from during control/low to during medium treatments (p=0.02, Figure 4C).

claim: Peduncle dives were the most common instantaneous event across phases for mothers (47%, 28 of 59 events).
source: Peduncle dives were the most common across phases (47%, 28 of 59 events), predominantly occurring during medium and high treatments (during low, 0%, 0 of 1 event; medium, 44%, 4 of 9 events; high, 73%, 8 of 11 events).
evidence: Stated as data summary

claim: There was no significant effect of treatment, phase or their interaction on the presence of events for the calf.
source: There was no significant effect of treatment, phase or their interaction on the presence of events for the calf (GLMM-PQL logit scale: R2(m) = 0.05, R2(c) = 0.33; 126 phases).

claim: The average respiration rate for the mother during control/low treatments was 0.3 (±0.12 SD) respirations min−1.
source: The average respiration rate for the mother during control/low treatments was 0.3 (±0.12 SD), during medium was 0.4 (±0.15 SD) and during high noise was 0.6 (±0.39 SD) respirations min−1.
evidence: Stated as measured data

claim: The average respiration rate for the mother during medium treatments was 0.4 (±0.15 SD) respirations min−1.
source: The average respiration rate for the mother during control/low treatments was 0.3 (±0.12 SD), during medium was 0.4 (±0.15 SD) and during high noise was 0.6 (±0.39 SD) respirations min−1.
evidence: Stated as measured data

claim: The average respiration rate for the mother during high noise was 0.6 (±0.39 SD) respirations min−1.
source: The average respiration rate for the mother during control/low treatments was 0.3 (±0.12 SD), during medium was 0.4 (±0.15 SD) and during high noise was 0.6 (±0.39 SD) respirations min−1.
evidence: Stated as measured data

source: For the respiration rate of the mother, within control/low and medium treatments, there were no significant effects across phases (LMM: R2(m) = 0.15, R2(c) = 0.46; 126 phases; Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

claim: Within the high treatments, the respiration rate from before to during vessel approaches increased significantly by 42% (p=0.001).
source: Within the high treatments, the respiration rate from before to during vessel approaches increased significantly by 42% (p=0.001, Figure 4D).
evidence: Stated as statistical result with reference to Figure 4D

claim: Among treatments, respiration rate during high noise was twice that of during control/low noise (p = <0.001).
source: Among treatments, respiration rate during high noise was twice that of during control/low noise (p = <0.001; Figure 4D).
evidence: Stated as statistical result with reference to Figure 4D

claim: Within medium noise, the mean heading change from before to after vessel approaches increased significantly by 29% (p=0.02).

claim: The mean speed of movement for the mother was 0.3 ms−1 (±0.17 SD) during medium noise.

claim: The mean speed of movement for the mother was 0.5 ms−1 (±0.36 SD) during high noise.
source: The mean speed of movement for the mother was 0.3 ms−1 (±0.24 SD) during control/low, 0.3 ms−1 (±0.17 SD) during medium and 0.5 ms−1 (±0.36 SD) during high noise.
evidence: Stated as measured data

source: Within high noise treatments, swim speed increased significantly by 33% from before to during vessel approaches (p=0.007).

source: Among treatments, swim speed during high noise increased significantly compared to during control/low treatments (p=0.04, 37% increase).

claim: Underwater noise level from a vessel, representative of motorised whale-watch vessels, is an adequate stimulus evoking disturbance from whale-watching on resting humpback whale mother-calf pairs on a resting ground.
source: Through controlled exposure experiments, we show that underwater noise level from a vessel, representative of motorised whale-watch vessels (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), is an adequate stimulus evoking disturbance from whale-watching on resting humpback whale mother-calf pairs on a resting ground.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: Humpback whale mothers rest on average for 35% of their time on the breeding ground.
source: Humpback whale mothers rest on average for 35% of their time on the breeding ground as the early phase of lactation is the most energetically demanding phase in their reproductive cycle, with females sometimes loosing >25% of their body condition in only 3–4 months (Christiansen et al., 2016a; Bejder et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Christiansen et al., 2016a and Bejder et al., 2019

claim: Humpback whale females sometimes lose >25% of their body condition in only 3–4 months during the early phase of lactation.
source: Humpback whale mothers rest on average for 35% of their time on the breeding ground as the early phase of lactation is the most energetically demanding phase in their reproductive cycle, with females sometimes loosing >25% of their body condition in only 3–4 months (Christiansen et al., 2016a; Bejder et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Christiansen et al., 2016a and Bejder et al., 2019

claim: Humpback whale calves nurse substantially (~20% of their time).
source: A calf is required to nurse substantially (~20% of their time; Videsen et al., 2017) to grow in strength and size (by ~3 cm in length a day; Christiansen et al., 2016a) within a short period of time to reduce predation (killer whales and sharks; Pitman et al., 2015) and endure the long migration to high latitude feeding grounds (Bestley et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Videsen et al., 2017

claim: Humpback whale calves grow by ~3 cm in length a day.
source: A calf is required to nurse substantially (~20% of their time; Videsen et al., 2017) to grow in strength and size (by ~3 cm in length a day; Christiansen et al., 2016a) within a short period of time to reduce predation (killer whales and sharks; Pitman et al., 2015) and endure the long migration to high latitude feeding grounds (Bestley et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Christiansen et al., 2016a

claim: Killer whales and sharks are predators of humpback whale calves.
source: A calf is required to nurse substantially (~20% of their time; Videsen et al., 2017) to grow in strength and size (by ~3 cm in length a day; Christiansen et al., 2016a) within a short period of time to reduce predation (killer whales and sharks; Pitman et al., 2015) and endure the long migration to high latitude feeding grounds (Bestley et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pitman et al., 2015

claim: For cetaceans hearing is the primary sensory modality which is more efficient than sight at longer ranges.
source: The demonstration that noise exposure level from a vessel is a driver of short-term behavioural disturbance in whales is perhaps not surprising, as for cetaceans hearing is the primary sensory modality which is more efficient than sight at longer ranges (Richardson et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citation to Richardson et al., 1995

claim: Cetacean sight underwater is highly limited and hence even under the best conditions they are unlikely to be able to see a vessel underwater at 100 m distance.
source: Cetacean sight underwater is highly limited and hence even under the best conditions they are unlikely to be able to see a vessel underwater at 100 m distance.
evidence: Based on general knowledge about cetacean vision and underwater visibility

claim: For vessels with spectral signatures similar to the playback used here, emission standards should be implemented so that vessels operating around whales as close as 100 m do not have LF-weighted SLs of more than 150 dB re 1 μPa RMS @ 1 m.
source: For humpback whales, we provide an evidence-based noise threshold for recommended application into global whale-watch guidelines: for vessels with spectral signatures similar to the playback used here, we suggest that emission standards be implemented so that vessels operating around whales as close as 100 m do not have LF-weighted SLs of more than 150 dB re 1 μPa RMS @ 1 m.
evidence: Recommendation based on experimental results

claim: Available data suggests a SL range from around 138 to 169 dB re 1 μPa @ 1 m for slow moving (<10 knts) whale-watch vessels.
source: Available data suggests a SL range from around 138 to 169 dB re 1 μPa @ 1 m for slow moving (<10 knts) whale-watch vessels (Au and Green, 2000; Jensen et al., 2009; Wladichuk et al., 2019), largely covering the low to high range of playback SLs used here.

claim: Operators can reduce the SL of their vessel by driving slowly.
